title: A Linear Model's Out-of-Fold Disagreements Are Mostly Label Errors: Dropping Them Beats a Larger Model Trained on Noisy Labels
insight: When a logistic regression trained on other folds disagrees with a sample's label, the label is usually wrong, so dropping those samples and refitting recovers most of the accuracy noise costs and beats an MLP that trains on every noisy label.
abstract_sketch: Methods for learning with noisy labels usually need a clean validation set, a noise-rate estimate or a deep network, and simple linear models have no plain filter of their own. We present an out-of-fold disagreement filter: fit logistic regression with 5-fold cross-validation, drop every training sample whose out-of-fold prediction disagrees with its given label, and refit on the rest. The key idea is that a sample which a model fit on the other folds cannot explain is more likely mislabeled than one it explains, so the model's own disagreement is a usable noise detector. On two small datasets with symmetric noise, most dropped samples are truly mislabeled, the refit model regains much of the accuracy that noise costs, and it beats an untuned MLP trained on the same noisy labels. With clean labels the filter costs a fraction of a point. The study is small and linear, and we make no claim about deep networks or large data.
figure1: Three panels with numbered circles. (1) A noisy training set as a grid of labeled points with a few flipped labels in red; (2) five folds, each predicted by a model fit on the other four, with samples that disagree with their label marked and removed (a small bar shows that most removed samples are truly flipped: precision); (3) grouped bars of test accuracy on digits at 40% noise: plain logistic regression, MLP (low, about 65%), filter (purple accent), and a gray 0%-noise logistic regression reference line. A reader sees the problem (noise drops accuracy), the mechanism (disagreement marks flips) and the result (filter above both baselines, near the clean reference) without the text. The caption states that digits at 40% noise is the largest-effect cell, and that breast cancer at 40% noise is smaller and unstable.
contributions: We present an out-of-fold disagreement filter for logistic regression that needs no clean validation set and uses no noise rate.
We show that the filter's drops are mostly truly mislabeled samples, that it recovers much of the accuracy lost to symmetric noise, and that it beats an untuned MLP trained on the same noisy labels.
We report where it does not help: the clean-label cost, the clean-label tie with the MLP, the unstable breast cancer 40% cell, and the scope of two small datasets with five seeds.
storyline: Label noise costs a plain linear model many accuracy points, and an untuned MLP falls much further, to about 65% at 40% noise. The observation that drives the paper is that the linear model's out-of-fold disagreements with the given labels are mostly real label errors. Across both datasets and both noise rates, the majority of dropped samples are flipped ones, and the filter removes most of the flipped labels. So the filter is just: cross-validate, drop the disagreements, refit, with no clean validation set and no noise rate. Dropping those samples recovers most of the lost accuracy in three of four noisy cells and beats the MLP in every noisy run, with gains that grow with noise on digits. The filter is not free or universal: it costs a fraction of a point on clean labels, the MLP is as good or slightly better there, and breast cancer at 40% noise recovers little and varies across seeds. This suggests that for simple models, the model's own held-out disagreement is a cheap, checkable noise detector, to be tested against confident learning and co-teaching and on larger models in future work.

risks: A reviewer will say the study is tiny (two sklearn datasets, five seeds), that the MLP is untuned so beating it proves little, that confident learning already uses out-of-fold predictions and co-teaching is not run, and that 'recovers most' fails on breast cancer at 40%. The paper answers by stating the scope up front, calling the MLP untuned and showing the clean-label tie, saying plainly that the filter is a simple linear instance of known out-of-fold ideas and that no head-to-head with confident learning was run, reporting the 22% recovery and the 9-point seed spread in that cell, and using the MLP's collapse only as a consistent-with observation (no memorization test was run).
